## Auth

JWT access token (short-lived, returned in the response body) + refresh token (long-lived, httpOnly cookie).

- `POST /api/v1/auth/register` — create an account
- `POST /api/v1/auth/login` — get a new access token + refresh cookie
- `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` — exchange the refresh cookie for a new access token
- `POST /api/v1/auth/logout` — clears the refresh cookie
- `GET /api/v1/auth/me` — current user (requires `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>`)

`register`/`login` are rate-limited (20 requests per 15 minutes per IP by default — see `middlewares/rateLimiter.js`) to blunt brute-force/mass-registration attempts.

`npm run seed` creates two test accounts (`admin@example.com` / `user@example.com`, both password `password123`) if they don't already exist, so `npm run dev` doesn't start against a totally empty database.

## Auth

JWT access token (short-lived, returned in the response body) + refresh token (long-lived, httpOnly cookie via `cookie-parser`).

- `POST /api/v1/auth/register` — create an account
- `POST /api/v1/auth/login` — get a new access token + refresh cookie
- `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` — exchange the refresh cookie for a new access token
- `POST /api/v1/auth/logout` — clears the refresh cookie
- `GET /api/v1/auth/me` — current user (requires `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>`)

`@nestjs/throttler` is registered app-wide (100 req/min default, in `AppModule`) via `APP_GUARD`; `register`/`login` override it with a tighter 20-per-15-minutes limit via `@Throttle(...)` (see `auth.controller.ts`) to blunt brute-force/mass-registration attempts.

`npm run seed` creates two test accounts (`admin@example.com` / `user@example.com`, both password `password123`) if they don't already exist, so `npm run dev` doesn't start against a totally empty database — connects directly via mongoose rather than bootstrapping the whole Nest app.

## Auth

JWT access token (short-lived, returned in the response body) + refresh token (long-lived, httpOnly cookie) — identical contract to the Mongoose-backed Auth module, just backed by Prisma/PostgreSQL instead. Password hashing happens explicitly in `auth.service.ts` (Prisma has no schema-level hooks the way Mongoose does, so there's no `pre("save", ...)` equivalent to hook into).

- `POST /api/v1/auth/register` — create an account
- `POST /api/v1/auth/login` — get a new access token + refresh cookie
- `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` — exchange the refresh cookie for a new access token
- `POST /api/v1/auth/logout` — clears the refresh cookie
- `GET /api/v1/auth/me` — current user (requires `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>`)

`register`/`login` are rate-limited (20 requests per 15 minutes per IP by default — see `middlewares/rateLimiter.ts`) to blunt brute-force/mass-registration attempts.

`npm run seed` creates two test accounts (`admin@example.com` / `user@example.com`, both password `password123`) if they don't already exist, so `npm run dev` doesn't start against a totally empty database.

## Database

MongoDB via Mongoose. Requires Node.js >=20.19.0 (Mongoose 9). Set `MONGO_URI` in `.env` (defaults to a local instance on 27017). The connection is opened in `loaders/index.js`, before the app is created — see that file for why. `GET /healthz` reports live connectivity (`mongoose.connection.readyState`); graceful shutdown (SIGTERM/SIGINT) closes the connection before the process exits. Note: `mongodb-memory-server` is included so tests can run against a real in-memory MongoDB without a local install, whether or not you also picked the testing module.

## Database

MongoDB via `@nestjs/mongoose`. Requires Node.js >=20.19.0 (Mongoose 9). Set `MONGO_URI` in `.env` (defaults to a local instance on 27017). Registered in `AppModule` via `MongooseModule.forRootAsync(...)` (async so tests can override `MONGO_URI` before the connection is opened); feature modules register their own schemas with `MongooseModule.forFeature(...)`. `GET /healthz` reports live connectivity; `app.enableShutdownHooks()` (in `main.ts`) makes Nest close the connection automatically on SIGTERM/SIGINT, no extra wiring needed. Note: `mongodb-memory-server` is included so tests can run against a real in-memory MongoDB without a local install, whether or not you also picked the testing module.

## Database

PostgreSQL via [Prisma](https://prisma.io) 7 — schema-first, with a fully typed client generated from `prisma/schema.prisma`. Requires Node.js `>=20.19.0`.

- `prisma/schema.prisma` — your data model. `predev`/`prebuild`/`pretest` all run `prisma generate` automatically, so the typed client stays in sync without a manual step.
- `prisma.config.ts` — where the CLI (`db:push`, `db:migrate`, `db:studio`) reads `DATABASE_URL` from; separate from the runtime client's driver adapter in `src/config/db.ts` (Prisma 7 requires an explicit adapter — `@prisma/adapter-pg` here — it no longer connects using the schema's `datasource.url` directly).
- Set `DATABASE_URL` in `.env` (defaults to a local Postgres on 5432). `npm run db:push` applies your schema to it without a full migration history — use `npm run db:migrate` instead once you want real, versioned migrations.
- The connection is opened in `src/loaders/index.ts`, before the app is created — see that file for why.
- `GET /healthz` reports live connectivity via a real `SELECT 1`; graceful shutdown (SIGTERM/SIGINT) calls `prisma.$disconnect()` before the process exits.
- Tests spin up a real, disposable Postgres container via [testcontainers](https://testcontainers.com) — see `src/test/global-setup.ts`/`global-teardown.ts` (Jest's `globalSetup`/`globalTeardown`, not `beforeAll`/`afterAll` in the test files themselves — starting a Docker-backed container from inside ts-jest's per-file ESM sandbox crashes on `docker-modem`'s bundled `readable-stream`; `globalSetup`/`globalTeardown` run in Jest's main process instead, outside that sandbox). `npm audit` will report vulnerabilities in this devDependency's own transitive tree (via `dockerode`) — they don't affect the shipped app (`npm audit --omit=dev` is clean); a newer `@testcontainers/postgresql` fixes them but requires Node ≥22.19.

## Logging

Winston, instead of the Pino default. `utils/logger.js` exports the same `logger.info/warn/error/fatal/debug` calls every other module in this project already uses, so nothing else needed to change when you picked this. `middlewares/requestLogger.js` replaces `pino-http` with an equivalent hand-rolled middleware (attaches `req.log`, logs one line per finished request). Note: `pino`/`pino-http`/`pino-pretty` stay listed in `package.json` since they're baked into the base template — they're unused here and safe to remove by hand if you want a leaner `node_modules`.

## RBAC (Permission-based)

A role maps to a list of permissions in `config/permissions.js`, and routes declare which permission they need:

```js
router.get("/admin-check", requireAuth, requirePermission("admin:access"), handler);
```

Add a new role, or change what an existing role can do, by editing `config/permissions.js` only. See `routes/admin.routes.js` for a working example (`GET /api/v1/admin-check`).

## Real-time (Socket.IO)

`useRealtime()` (from `src/realtime/RealtimeContext.jsx`) connects to the backend composer's `realtime-socketio*` module and shows a live "who's online" list — pair the two and it works out of the box, same as the Auth module.

- The socket only opens once `useAuth()` has an `accessToken` — Socket.IO's handshake carries it as `auth: { token }`, matching the backend's expectation, and closes automatically on logout.
- `presence:update` events (broadcast whenever anyone joins/leaves) update `online`, an array of `{ id, name }` for everyone currently connected — `PresenceList` in `src/components/` renders it, and is what's dropped into `src/App.jsx` by default.

Set `VITE_SOCKET_URL` in `.env` to your backend's *origin* (no path — defaults to `http://localhost:4000`, matching the backend composer's default port). This is deliberately separate from `VITE_API_URL` (which includes `/api/v1`): Socket.IO connects directly to the server origin and does its own path-based routing (`/socket.io/`) underneath.

esm.readme:
## Real-time (Socket.IO)

A live "who's online" presence demo, authenticated with the exact same JWT the HTTP API uses.

- The client connects with `io(url, { auth: { token: accessToken } })` — Socket.IO's handshake has no header the client can set before the WebSocket upgrade, so the access token travels as a handshake auth payload instead of an `Authorization` header.
- `sockets/index.js`'s `io.use(...)` middleware verifies that token with the same `verifyAccessToken` the HTTP `requireAuth` middleware uses, and rejects the connection (`connect_error`) if it's missing or invalid.
- On a successful connection, the socket joins a shared `lobby` room and the server broadcasts `presence:update` with the current list of connected users to everyone in that room — try opening two browser tabs logged in as different users.
- Presence is tracked in memory (a `Map`), so it resets on server restart and doesn't scale past one server process — swap in a Redis adapter (`@socket.io/redis-adapter`) if you need multiple server instances.

A live "who's online" presence demo, authenticated with the exact same JWT the HTTP API uses.

- The client connects with `io(url, { auth: { token: accessToken } })` — Socket.IO's handshake has no header the client can set before the WebSocket upgrade, so the access token travels as a handshake auth payload instead of an `Authorization` header.

## Styling

[Ant Design](https://ant.design) backs `src/components/{Button,Input,Modal,Spinner}.jsx` — `Button`/`Input`/`Modal`/`Spinner` wrap antd's own. Note antd's `Button` `type` prop means style variant, not HTML button type, so the wrapper maps our `type` to antd's `htmlType` for you. Every other module (`auth-react`, `router-react`, `state-zustand`, ...) only ever imports from `./components/*`, so it works unchanged no matter which styling library is picked — this is the one place Ant Design is actually wired in.

A real `ConfigProvider` (`theme: { algorithm: darkAlgorithm | defaultAlgorithm }`) lives in `src/theme/ThemeContext.jsx`, driven by the same light/dark/system `ThemeToggle` (antd's own `Segmented` + `@ant-design/icons`) every styling option ships.

It deliberately skips `CssBaseline` — that would overwrite the gradient hero background from `index.css` with MUI's own flat background color.

jsx.readme:
## Styling

[Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com) is set up via `tailwind.config.js` / `postcss.config.js`, with the `@tailwind` directives in `src/index.css`. `src/components/{Button,Input,Modal,Spinner}.jsx` are styled with Tailwind utility classes (including `dark:` variants) — every other module (`auth-react`, `router-react`, `state-zustand`, ...) only ever imports from `./components/*`, so it works unchanged no matter which styling library is picked. Restyle any of them further any time; the plain `components.css` from the base is no longer used once Tailwind is selected.

`tailwind.config.js` sets `darkMode: "class"`, and this module's own `src/theme/ThemeContext.jsx` toggles that `dark` class on `<html>` alongside the shared `data-theme` attribute — so the base's light/dark/system `ThemeToggle` also drives any `dark:` utility classes you add yourself, not just the ones already here.
